claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a protective passive film enriched in chromium and molybdenum.
The Cr/Mo-enriched passive film forms through preferential oxidation during service exposure.
Grain-boundary carbide precipitates stabilize the passive film by acting as diffusion barriers.
In nuclear environments, irradiation-induced defects may provide nucleation sites for passive-film repair and improve self-healing.
316-type austenitic stainless steel typically contains approximately 16–18 wt.% Cr and 2–3 wt.% Mo.
Typical cast or rolled 316-type steel contains grain-boundary carbides and undissolved inclusions.
Heat treatments can be designed to enhance Cr/Mo segregation and carbide formation in the tested steel.
An acidic, chloride-containing solution at 80°C is representative of chemical-processing corrosion conditions.
High-purity water at approximately 300°C under controlled potential is representative of nuclear-reactor coolant conditions.
The governing structural mediator is a dense, Cr/Mo-enriched surface oxide augmented by grain-boundary carbides.
Grain-boundary carbides facilitate and stabilize the elemental segregation needed for rapid repassivation.
Preferential oxidation of chromium, and to a lesser extent molybdenum, produces a continuous and adherent passive film with low ionic conductivity.
Carbide precipitates promote local Cr/Mo enrichment, accelerating passive-film formation and increasing film stability.
Microstructures optimized for Cr/Mo segregation will produce lower corrosion rates than the baseline microstructure.
Microstructures optimized for Cr/Mo segregation will produce higher breakdown potentials and faster repassivation than baseline samples.
Low-dose irradiation will improve maintenance of passive-film integrity relative to non-irradiated controls.
The proposed mechanism should apply to steels containing approximately 10–25 wt.% Cr and 1–3 wt.% Mo under chemical-processing or reactor-coolant conditions.
The proposed mechanism may fail at very high acid concentrations, at irradiation levels substantially above service values, or in radically different steel compositions.
